title: Serving Runtime: Architecture, Kernel Scheduling, Profiling & Runbooks
author: Aisha Patel
content:
Overview

This document consolidates the serving runtime architecture, kernel scheduling strategy, profiling and benchmarking playbooks, recent release notes, known issues, on-call runbooks, and team wiki pointers for the eng-serving-runtime area. It is the canonical reference for engineers and SREs responsible for inference performance, stability, and capacity.

Goals:
- Provide a single reference for architecture and scheduling design decisions.
- Define concrete profiling, repro, and benchmarking steps for troubleshooting regressions.
- Capture operational runbooks for common incidents (latency, OOMs, GPU faults).
- Build reproducible benchmark artifacts and a consistent release note pattern.

Ownership and contacts
- Runtime core team: eng/runtime (owner).
- On-call rota: runtime-oncall@redwood.internal (see team wiki for schedule).
- Pager escalation: page SRE on-call after 15 minutes if not acknowledged.

1) Runtime architecture (high level)

Summary: Redwood's serving runtime is a modular, GPU-optimized inference engine that exposes a consistent API across Hosted / Dedicated / Private deployments. Key subsystems: request ingress, router & policy layer, batching & kernel scheduler, model execution (kernels + quantized VM), KV cache, result aggregator, and observability hooks.

Diagram (textual):
- Ingress (HTTP/gRPC) -> Auth & Quotas -> Router (policy: latency/cost/region) -> Batching layer -> Kernel scheduler -> Model execution (CUDA / ROCm / XLA paths) -> KV cache lookup/update -> Output post-processing -> Metrics & tracing -> Response.

Key design principles:
- Predictable latency: isolate low-latency routes (chat) from throughput-heavy batch jobs via route-level policies.
- Cost efficiency: automatic batching + KV caching to reduce per-token GPU work.
- Graceful degradation: fallback to smaller/quantized model variants under load.
- Observability-first: token-level tracing, batch composition logs, kernel-level counters.

SLOs and targets (service-level):
- 95th percentile end-to-end request latency: 
  - small models (<=2B params): <= 250 ms
  - medium models (2B-13B): <= 600 ms
  - large models (>13B): <= 1.8 s
- p99 latency: capped at 2x the 95th target for each class.
- Availability: 99.95% monthly uptime for Hosted API endpoints.
- Error rate: API error rate < 0.1% (5xx).

2) Kernel scheduling and batching strategy

Goals: maximize GPU utilization while respecting latency SLOs for prioritized traffic.

Core concepts:
- Continuous batching: form batches incrementally; send to GPU when either batch size threshold or max wait threshold is reached.
- Priority lanes: high-priority, latency-sensitive requests are isolated to separate queues with tighter max-wait thresholds.
- Fallback preemption: if high-priority requests arrive while a large batch is forming, the scheduler can preempt or split batches depending on model compatibility.
- Kernel selection: use model metadata (seq length distribution, head count) to choose optimized kernels and quantization-friendly paths at runtime.

Important parameters (default values):
- max_batch_size: 32 (small models), 8 (large models)
- max_queue_wait_ms: 15 ms (high-priority), 60 ms (background throughput)
- max_active_batches_per_gpu: 2

Batch formation policy (step-by-step):
1. Request arrives and is classified by route/model.
2. Inserted into per-model, per-priority queue.
3. A background batcher collects requests: stops when batch size hits max_batch_size OR oldest_request_wait_ms >= max_queue_wait_ms.
4. Batches are scheduled to GPU if they fit into current active batch windows; otherwise queued to next window.
5. If a higher-priority request would exceed latency SLO, preemption logic attempts to split or reassign batching windows.

Tradeoffs and tuning guidance:
- Increasing max_batch_size improves GPU throughput but increases tail latency - tune per-model using the benchmark harness.
- Aggressive preemption improves latency SLOs but reduces GPU efficiency due to smaller batches.
- Kernel choice can materially affect memory footprint; prefer fused kernels for large-seq workloads.

3) Profiling playbook (how to reproduce and debug perf regressions)

When a performance regression or unpredictable latency is detected, follow the steps below. The playbook is intentionally prescriptive to accelerate reliable root cause analysis.

Quick triage checklist:
1. Confirm scope: single request route? model family? region? customer?
2. Check dashboards: batch size distributions, KV cache hit-rate, GPU util, mem alloc, compiler cache hit/miss.
3. If p95/p99 latency increased, capture traces for 10 affected requests (trace-id list).

Full profiling steps:
1. Reproduce locally or in a staging cluster with same model and workload settings. Use the benchmark harness (see section 4) with matching seq lengths and prompt mixes.
2. Collect system-level metrics: nvidia-smi dmon, DCGM, /proc/meminfo, iostat. Capture a 60-second window covering the spike.
3. Collect runtime traces: enable token-level tracing (TRACE_LEVEL=request) for the route; collect batch composition logs.
4. Kernel-level profiling: run Nsight Systems or Nsight Compute against the exact model binary and with the same input shapes. For CUDA: nsight-sys --target-processes all --capture-range ...; nsight-cu for kernel hotspots.
5. Check memory allocator metrics: device heap fragmentation, peak allocation, and caching behavior (cudaMalloc vs caching allocator).
6. Verify KV cache metrics: hit ratio, eviction churn, average cached prefix length.

Essential commands (examples):
- Capture DCGM metrics: dcgmi stats -i 0 --group "GPU_Utilization,SM,Memory" --sample-interval 1000 --samples 60
- Nsight Systems quick record:
  nsys profile --capture-range=chrono --target-pid <pid> --output /tmp/trace %SERVICE_COMMAND%
- Collect runtime batch logs: curl -H "X-Debug-Tracing: true" 'http://localhost:8080/debug/batches?last_minutes=10'

Profiling outputs to attach to incidents:
- batch-logs.tar.gz (batch composition + timings)
- nsight-sys trace (.qdrep) and summarized hotspots (.csv)
- DCGM + node-metrics (JSON)
- model kernel flamegraph (SVG)

4) Benchmarking suite and reproducible workloads

Benchmark harness objectives: measure latency-throughput curves for representative workload mixes, validate kernel selection choices, and quantify cost per token. Benchmarks must be run with pinned model versions and deterministic seeds.

Standard benchmark workloads (examples):
- chat-short: 80% short prompt (<64 tokens), 20% single-turn generation (<=128 tokens)
- chat-long: 40% prompts <64, 60% multi-turn sessions with avg generated tokens=512
- embed-cold: embedding single-shot requests of size 512 tokens
- rerank: batched scoring of 16 candidates with 128-token contexts

Required benchmark configuration table (text):
- model: model-id (e.g., redwood/airo-13b-fp16)
- hardware: GPU type & driver (e.g., A100-40GB, CUDA 12.1)
- batcher: max_batch_size, max_queue_wait_ms
- sequence-distribution: mean/median length
- concurrency: requests/sec target and number of client workers
- seed: deterministic RNG seed for generation

Run a representative benchmark: (example command)
- ./bench/runner --model redwood/airo-13b-fp16 --hardware A100-40GB --workload chat-long --duration 10m --concurrency 64 --output results.json

Benchmark outputs:
- latency percentiles (p50, p95, p99), throughput (tokens/sec), GPU utilization, cost-per-token estimate.

5) Release notes (runtime component)

Pattern and example entries: always include version, date, summary, impact, rollback instructions, and owners.

- v2026.11.18 - 2026-11-18
  - Summary: Kernel selection heuristic updated to prefer fused attention for seq_len > 1024 on A100.
  - Impact: expected 12-28% throughput improvement on long-context workloads.
  - Rollback: set env KERNEL_OVERRIDE=fallback-attn and restart runtime service.
  - Owners: Maya Chen (runtime), Ravi Narayanan (perf).

- v2026.11.30 - 2026-11-30
  - Summary: Fix for memory leak in quantized matmul path (addr issue #1423).
  - Impact: reduced OOM incidents during high-concurrency tests.
  - Rollback: revert release commit %SHA% and redeploy.

6) Known issues (current, and workarounds)

- Issue: p99 latency regressions on medium models when mixing seq lengths.
  - Symptom: sudden spikes in p99 while p95 remains steady.
  - Root cause: batch fragmentation due to heterogeneous seq-lengths triggering less-efficient kernels.
  - Workaround: enforce per-route shape bucketing (route-config: shape_buckets=[64,256,512]) and set max_queue_wait_ms=30 for medium models.

- Issue: intermittent GPU kernel timeouts on older drivers.
  - Workaround: upgrade to CUDA 12.1+ and driver 535+; if not possible, set KERNEL_TIMEOUT_MS=20000 to allow longer runtime windows.

- Issue: KV cache thrashing for multi-turn sessions with frequent prompt variation.
  - Workaround: increase kv_cache_capacity for affected customers or enable sessionpinning to the same worker.

7) Runtime runbooks (operational recipes)

Runbook: High 95th/99th latency spike
1. Triage: Check dashboards (per-route latency, batch sizes, queue wait times, GPU util).
2. If batch_size << configured max: suspect preemption or high-priority traffic - check batch composition logs.
3. If GPU util is high and latency is high: identify kernel hotspot with nsight traces; consider bursting to dedicated pool or scaling out.
4. Short term mitigation: enable route-level throttle or fallback to smaller model variant.
5. Post-incident: collect traces, run bench harness to reproduce, file perf regression PR.

Runbook: OOM on GPU during peak
1. Confirm OOM logs from runtime: check stderr for CUDA OOM and core dump.
2. Capture device memory usage timeline (nvidia-smi dmon).
3. If caused by model change: roll back to previous model build and redeploy.
4. Mitigations: lower max_batch_size, enable mixed-precision (fp16) path, increase swap/headroom via warmup containers.

Runbook: Worker / GPU crash (fatal)
1. Mark worker as drained in scheduler, re-route traffic.
2. Collect system logs, dmesg, kernel OOPS, and GPU driver logs.
3. If reproducible, escalate to infra and driver teams with trace and binary.

8) Team wiki and operational artifacts

Links and pages to keep updated:
- Runtime team wiki (roles, oncall rota, Slack channels): /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/team-wiki
- Bench harness repo: git@internal:redwood/serving-bench.git (branch: main)
- Model onboarding checklist: /confluence/applied-ml-and-evals/model-onboarding
- Observability dashboards: Grafana -> cluster:runtime-overview; Traces -> Jaeger:runtime

Onboarding checklist for new runtime engineers:
1. Read this doc and runtime architecture overview.
2. Run the bench harness locally against a small model.
3. Shadow on-call for at least two weeks and review all runbooks.
4. Complete runtime kata: reproduce and fix a synthetic regression in a staging cluster.

Appendix: Useful snippets
- Example curl request (debug mode):
  curl -X POST \n    -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \n    -H "Content-Type: application/json" \n    -H "X-Debug-Tracing: true" \n    -d '{"model":"redwood/airo-7b","input":"Hello world","max_tokens":64}' \n    https://api.redwood.example/v1/generate

- Shape bucketing config example (route YAML):
  route:
    name: chat-medium
    model: redwood/airo-13b-fp16
    batching:
      max_batch_size: 16
      max_queue_wait_ms: 25
      shape_buckets: [64, 256, 512]

Document maintenance
- This doc is reviewed monthly by the runtime owners and updated after every major release.
- For additions or corrections, open a PR against the confluence source repo or email the runtime-owner alias.
